position_in_era.primary_genre_lineage: NYC punk/new wave deliberately crossing into disco
position_in_era.historical_role: A punk-scene band recorded a track built around a Roland CR-78 drum machine -- hardware released that same year -- and fused it with a disco arrangement, enacting the same rock-to-disco translation as Miss You in the same calendar year but from the opposite starting point of punk credibility.

narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Debbie Harry and Chris Stein had written an embryonic version called Once I Had a Love as early as 1974-75, but the song resisted every format they tried -- ballad, reggae -- until producer Mike Chapman heard the potential and pushed for a full disco treatment that the rest of the band, with their punk identities, found uncomfortable.
narrative_slots.production_facts: Chris Stein and keyboardist Jimmy Destri purchased a Roland CR-78 rhythm machine from a store on 47th Street in Manhattan and brought it into the session at the Record Plant; it was only the second year the device existed on the market. Producer Mike Chapman spent two months assembling the Parallel Lines tracks with the band in June-July 1978.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: The song fused what critics described as Blondie's NYC punk stance with sleek sequenced disco at a moment when the two scenes were still considered diametrically opposed, making the track a flashpoint for debates about authenticity and genre crossing that exactly mirrored the tensions around Miss You.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Released as the third single from Parallel Lines in January 1979, reaching number one on both the US Billboard Hot 100 and the UK Singles Chart.
